hints: Find the two separate masses from the $750 \text{ g}$ total: $60\%$ magnesium and $40\%$ copper.
Recall $\rho = m/V$ rearranged to $V = m/\rho$, so the low-density magnesium contributes a much larger volume than the copper.
Add the two volumes to get the block volume, then calculate $\rho = 750 \text{ g} / V_{total}$ and check the unit $\text{g cm}^{-3}$.
walkthrough: Mass of magnesium is $m_{Mg} = 0.60 \times 750 = 450 \text{ g}$ and mass of copper is $m_{Cu} = 750 - 450 = 300 \text{ g}$.
Use $V = m/\rho$ for each metal. For magnesium $V_{Mg} = 450/1.7 \approx 264.7 \text{ cm}^{3}$.
For copper $V_{Cu} = 300/9.0 \approx 33.3 \text{ cm}^{3}$, much smaller because copper is denser.
Total volume is $V = V_{Mg} + V_{Cu} \approx 264.7 + 33.3 \approx 298.0 \text{ cm}^{3}$.
Density of block is $\rho = m_{total}/V = 750/298.0 \approx 2.5 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$. This is option A.

options.A: Total mass $750 \text{ g}$ divided by total volume about $298 \text{ cm}^{3}$ gives about $2.5 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$.
options.B: This is the mass-weighted mean $0.6 \times 1.7 + 0.4 \times 9.0$, but densities cannot be averaged by mass because volumes add, not densities.
options.C: This is close to the simple mean of $1.7$ and $9.0$, which ignores the different masses and the different volumes of the two metals.
options.D: This is the sum $1.7 + 9.0$, but density of a mixture is total mass divided by total volume and cannot exceed both component densities.
